The committee-to-second-reading column is darker in every period, indicating that position changes concentrate between the committee vote and the floor."} ::: # Context In [Part I of this post](https://werk.statt.codes/posts/2026-05-21-ParlAT-votingPatterns/), I showcased how the {ParlAT} package offers some simple, yet powerful means to analyze voting behavior of parties in the Austrian National Council. The analysis detailed how parties voted (for or against) and on the frequency of party-combinations, i.e. how often e.g. party A voted with party B. All of the presented analysis dealt with the votes in the third reading, that is, at the last stage of the legislative procedure in the National Council. In this post I want to expand the analysis beyond the third reading and include the earlier stages of the legislative process in the National Council as well: the committee (Ausschuss), the second reading and the third reading. While doing this my interest is not so much how a party voted at a specific stage, but more on whether and *how often party positions on a legislative item actually changed over the course of the different stages within the National Council*. With this general interest a number of other questions lend themselves to being answered: - between which stages (committee → second reading, second → third reading) do the most changes happen? - how do parties differ when it comes to the frequency of changing their voting position over the course of different stages? - during which government can we observe most vote changes? On a conceptual level, I believe that answering these questions can contribute to a better understanding of how government parties respond to opposition demands. Strictly speaking, a change of vote could also simply mean that an opposition party changed its mind after further consideration. While that is possible, it is unlikely; in most cases a change of an opposition party's vote means that the party got something in return. Whether this was indeed a change in the content of the bill at stake, or on another, unrelated issue, can't be answered without looking into the details of the specific item. But retrieving these numbers is a first step. Two conceptual notes of caution: - *Absolute numbers can mislead.* For a flip from no to yes to materialize we need to have a 'no' in the first place. If there never was a 'no', i.e. if a bill enjoyed unanimous support from the start, there cannot be any flip either. But in that case, the absence of a flip obviously does not indicate a lack of government responsiveness. - **Legislative periods aren't directly comparable.** Different legislative periods have different legislative items at play, and these may vary in their level of contestation, i.e. how difficult it is for government and opposition parties to find common ground. Not every legislative period brings up items of similar levels of contestation. # Set-up Get the necessary packages. In addition, I define here a small helper function which gives all reactable tables in this post a consistent look (title, optional subtitle, and a source note at the bottom), so I don't have to repeat the same styling code over and over again. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Load packages"} library(ParlAT) library(tidyverse) library(furrr) library(reactable) library(reactablefmtr) library(naniar) library(ggtext) # shared table theme and attribution footer for all reactable tables compact_table_theme <- reactablefmtr::fivethirtyeight(font_size = 12) table_source <- reactablefmtr::html( "Source: www.parlament.gv.at. Analysis: Roland Schmidt - @zoowalk.bsky.social - https://werk.statt.codes" ) # helper that wraps any reactable with a consistent title, optional subtitle, and source footer style_reactable_table <- function(table, title, subtitle = NULL) { styled_table <- table %>% reactablefmtr::add_title( title = reactablefmtr::html(paste0( "", title, "" )) ) if (!is.null(subtitle)) { styled_table <- styled_table %>% reactablefmtr::add_subtitle( subtitle = reactablefmtr::html(paste0( "", subtitle, "" )), font_color = "grey30", font_weight = "normal", font_style = "italic" ) } styled_table %>% reactablefmtr::add_source(source = table_source) } ``` ::: # Get Data ## Data on the readings This section assembles the first half of the dataset: the bills themselves and the stage data recorded on their own pages, which is where the second- and third-reading votes live. The other half — the committee vote, which as we'll see is *not* recorded there — follows in the next section, and the two are brought together after that. ### Query the items As in the previous post, let's start by getting the government bills ('Regierungsvorlagen') of the National Council for the legislative periods 20 to 28. With {ParlAT}. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Fetch National Council government bills and cache them"} # fetch RV (Regierungsvorlagen) for legislative periods 20–28 (GP XX through XXVIII) items_20_28 <- seq(20, 28) %>% map(., \(x) get_items(item = "RV", legis_period = x, institution = "NR")) %>% list_rbind() # stack per-period tibbles into one dataframe # guard against overwriting a good cache with an empty/failed fetch if (nrow(items_20_28) == 0) { stop("The RV fetch returned no rows; the existing items cache was not overwritten.") } readr::write_rds( items_20_28, here::here( "posts", "2026-06-08-ParlAT-votingPatterns-2", "_data", "items_20_28.rds" ) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} nrow(items_20_28) ## [1] 2710 ``` ::: ### Query the stages Now let's feed the URLs of the obtained items to `get_item_details()`, this time with the `stages` parameter set to `TRUE`. The stages data contains one row per procedural step of an item, and — crucially for this post — the description of each voting step. As in the previous post, I wrap the function call in purrr's `safely()` to collect any potential errors without breaking the loop, and use `future_map()` to query the API with multiple workers simultaneously, i.e. to speed up the process. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show" code-summary="Fetch item details with stages and cache them"} plan(multisession, workers = 4) # parallelise across 4 cores to speed up API fetching item_urls <- items_20_28 %>% pull(item_url) # wrap in safely() so a single failed request returns an error slot instead of halting the loop safe_get_item_details <- safely(get_item_details) item_details_raw <- item_urls %>% future_map( \(x) { safe_result <- safe_get_item_details(item_url = x, stages = TRUE) safe_result$item_url <- x # attach URL so failed results can be identified later safe_result }, .progress = TRUE, .options = furrr_options(packages = c("ParlAT", "purrr", "tibble")) ) plan(sequential) # reset to single-threaded after parallel fetch # don't overwrite a good cache if every request failed item_success_n <- sum(map_lgl(item_details_raw, \(x) is.null(x$error))) if (item_success_n == 0) { stop(paste0( "All ", length(item_details_raw), " item-detail requests failed; the existing cache was not overwritten. ", "First error: ", conditionMessage(item_details_raw[[1]]$error) )) } # persist the raw fetch results so re-renders don't need to re-hit the API readr::write_rds( item_details_raw, here::here( "posts", "2026-06-08-ParlAT-votingPatterns-2", "_data", "item_details_raw.rds" ) ) ``` ::: ### Prepare stages data Below, I a) check for any failed calls, and b) combine the successful calls into a single data frame. Subsequently, I unnest the stages column so that we get one row per procedural step per item. Note that at this point the data frame still contains *all* stage rows for each item — also those without any vote. Filtering for the actual votes comes next. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Combine successful fetches and unnest stages into one row per step"} # collect items where the API call failed; conditionMessage() extracts the error string failed_items <- item_details_raw |> keep(\(x) !is.null(x$error)) |> map(\(x) tibble(item_url = x$item_url, error = conditionMessage(x$error))) |> list_rbind() failed_items ## data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows # keep only successful results and extract the nested $result element item_details <- item_details_raw |> keep(\(x) is.null(x$error)) |> map("result") |> list_rbind() # unnest stages into one row per stage per item item_stages <- item_details |> select( item_url, legis_period, type_doc, title, item_number, status_number, status_description, stages ) |> filter(map_lgl(stages, \(x) !is.null(x))) |> # drop items with no stage data at all unnest(stages) %>% mutate(stage_date = lubridate::dmy(stage_date)) # used in inline text and table subtitles throughout the document. # Two guards: na.rm, because a single unparseable date would otherwise render every # "Data as of ..." line as "NA"; and the cap at today's date, because the stages table # also carries *scheduled* future sittings. Taking a plain maximum would date the whole # post weeks ahead of the last vote actually recorded in it. data_cutoff <- max( item_stages$stage_date[item_stages$stage_date <= Sys.Date()], na.rm = TRUE ) ``` ::: The screenshot in the margin is from the website of the Parliament and shows the details on the different stages of one specific bill — the same kind of information we just retrieved with the code chunk above. Two things are worth flagging up front. First, at this point we have data on *all* stages, not only voting results; rows we're not interested in still need to be dropped. Second, and this is something what we have to take care off further below, the stage data does not contain any info on the committee's own vote — that lives in a different entry, the one belonging to the committee's report on the bill. To make this concrete, the *example* below follows one specific bill end to end, through every transformation step in this post: a 2024 amendment to the Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz (the renewable-energy-expansion act). It's a good running example precisely because it isn't a straightforward case: the FPÖ moves from opposing it in committee to supporting it by the second reading, and the SPÖ opposes it through the second reading before coming around at the third — so we'll be able to watch both kinds of position change appear in the data as the pipeline builds up. Querying the bill's own page with `get_item_details(stages = TRUE)` returns the stages shown in the screenshot and table below. ::: {.column-margin} ![The bill's own page on the Parliament's website, listing its stages. Click to enlarge. [link](https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608){target="_blank"}](_img/NRStagesErneuerbar.png) ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false" code-summary="Get every recorded stage for the example item"} # the one bill this post follows end to end through every transformation step below example_item_url <- "https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608" item_stages_example <- get_item_details(item_url = example_item_url, stages = TRUE) %>% select( item_url, legis_period, type_doc, stages, title, item_number, status_number, status_description ) |> filter(map_lgl(stages, \(x) !is.null(x))) |> # drop items with no stage data at all unnest(stages) %>% mutate(stage_date = lubridate::dmy(stage_date)) %>% select(phase, stage_name, stage_date, item_url) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false" code-summary="Item stages"} item_stages_example ## # A tibble: 30 × 4 ## phase stage_name stage_date item_url ## ## 1 Einlangen NR "Einlangen im Nationalrat" 2024-06-12 https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608 ## 2 Einlangen NR "Gesetzesvorschlag enthält Verfassungsbestimmungen" 2024-06-12 https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608 ## 3 Einlangen NR "Mehrheit von zwei Dritteln der abgegebenen Stimmen erforderlich" 2024-06-12 https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608 ## 4 Einlangen NR "Vorgesehen für den Ausschuss für Wirtschaft, Industrie und Energie" 2024-06-12 https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608 ## 5 Einlangen NR "267. From these rows we will later keep only the rows containing relevant votes for the second and third reading; and subsequently extract from these rows the voting decisions for each individual party. Contrasting the obtained results between the different readings allows identifying whether a party changed its position over the course of the legislative proceedings in the National Council. ## Committee reports While we have now all available data which is included in the stage data of a legislative item, it turns out that there is a gap on the votes casted in the committees. It is worth pausing on what the item's own page records about its committee phase, because, as it turns out, surprisingly little of it is the actual vote. A committee does far more than decide on a bill: it requests written opinions (Stellungnahmen), sets deadlines (Fristsetzungen), refers items back, and so on. The table below breaks all of a bill's National Council committee stages down by type. *The conclusion: the formal adoption vote, the committee's decision on the bill, the part we actually want, appears on the bill's own page only rarely. That is exactly why the rest of this section goes after the committee reports and takes the committee vote from there instead.* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Categorise National Council committee stages and show the vote share"} # same vote-keyword set the scope filter below relies on committee_vote_keywords <- "dafür|wechselnde Mehrheit|getrennte Abstimmung|namentliche Abstimmung|abgelehnt|mehrstimmig" # classify every National Council committee stage by what it records committee_stages <- item_stages %>% filter(phase == "Ausschussberatungen NR") %>% mutate( is_vote = str_detect( stage_name, regex(committee_vote_keywords, ignore_case = TRUE) ), category = case_when( str_detect( stage_name, regex("Antrag auf Annahme des", ignore_case = TRUE) ) ~ "Adoption vote on the bill", str_detect( stage_name, regex("Einholung einer Stellungnahme", ignore_case = TRUE) ) ~ "Opinion request (Stellungnahme)", str_detect(stage_name, regex("Fristsetzung", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Deadline motion (Fristsetzung)", is_vote ~ "Other vote", .default = "Non-vote / procedural" ), # flags the committee's formal adoption vote. Note this is *not* the row that reaches # the analysis: the committee position is taken from the committee report instead # (see below), because the bill's own page records the adoption vote only rarely is_adoption_vote = category == "Adoption vote on the bill" ) # aggregate to one row per category with its share of all committee stages committee_category_summary <- committee_stages %>% summarise(rows = n(), .by = c(category, is_adoption_vote)) %>% mutate( share = rows / sum(rows), is_adoption_vote_label = if_else(is_adoption_vote, "Yes", "No") ) %>% arrange(desc(rows)) %>% select(category, rows, share, is_adoption_vote_label) committee_category_table <- reactable( committee_category_summary, columns = list( category = colDef(name = "Committee stage type", minWidth = 230), rows = colDef( name = "Stages", align = "right", minWidth = 90, format = colFormat(separators = TRUE) ), share = colDef( name = "Share of committee stages", minWidth = 230, align = "left", # data bars make the tiny vote share read at a glance against the procedural bulk cell = reactablefmtr::data_bars( committee_category_summary, max_value = 1, number_fmt = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1), fill_color = "#1a9641", background = "#f0f0f0", text_position = "outside-end" ) ), is_adoption_vote_label = colDef( name = "Adoption vote?", align = "center", minWidth = 130 ) ), fullWidth = TRUE, compact = TRUE, highlight = TRUE, outlined = TRUE, theme = compact_table_theme ) %>% style_reactable_table( "WHAT THE BILL'S OWN PAGE RECORDS ABOUT ITS COMMITTEE PHASE", paste0( "All committee stages recorded on the bills' own pages, by type — the adoption vote is the rarest of them. ``` ::: ::: Across all 10,438 committee stages recorded on the bills' own pages, only 0.9% record a vote at all, and just 0.4% are the bill-adoption vote — which is why the committee position is taken from the committee report rather than from these rows. ### Linking a report to its bill To demonstrate how to get the committee voting data, let's now fetch the example bill's companion report page the same way, with `get_item_details()`, and look at what it carries. Besides `stages`, every item, bill or report alike, also carries a `references` column: a list of typed cross-references to other legislative objects. That column is the mechanism to link a committee vote back to its bill. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show" code-summary="Fetch the committee report's own page and show its references, incl. the Hauptgegenstand (HG) link back to the bill"} example_report_url <- "https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2666" item_report_example <- get_item_details( item_url = example_report_url, stages = TRUE ) item_references_example <- item_report_example %>% select(references) %>% unnest(references) %>% select(text, subject, zitation, url, art) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false" code-summary="Report references"} item_references_example ## # A tibble: 1 × 5 ## text subject zitation url art ## ## 1 Hauptgegenstand des Berichts Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz, Änderung 2608 d.B. /gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608 HG ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} # resolve the HG row's relative url into the same absolute form item_url uses elsewhere hg_parent_url <- item_references_example %>% filter(art == "HG") %>% mutate(parent_url = paste0("https://www.parlament.gv.at", url)) %>% pull(parent_url) hg_parent_url ## [1] "https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608" ``` ::: The report carries a single reference row here, typed `HG`. Its `url` resolves to https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608 — exactly the `item_url` of the bill's own stages table shown further above. That one row is the entire link between the two datasets: a committee report holds no bill-specific vote information anywhere else, and a bill's own page holds no back-reference to its report at all. `art` is how the Parliament's data model types these cross-references; besides `HG`, a report can also carry `MG` ('Mitgegenstand', a co-subject bundled into the same report) and, more rarely, `HGS`, `ZU` or `B` for other bundling or referral cases — but only `HG` is used as the match key below. ### Fetch the committee reports With the link understood, we can go and get the reports themselves. The object holding the committee's adoption vote is the committee report (`Ausschussbericht`, type `AUB`): it carries the formal `Antrag auf Annahme des Gesetzesvorschlags` section (the motion to adopt the bill), which includes each party's vote, plus the `HG` reference back to the parent bill we just followed. So to capture committee votes properly, I fetch every committee report for periods 20–28 with its own targeted `get_items()` call, again with `stages = TRUE`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Fetch all committee reports (Ausschussbericht) with stages and cache them"} aub_urls <- seq(20, 28) %>% map(., \(x) get_items(item = "AUB", legis_period = x, institution = "NR")) %>% list_rbind() %>% pull(item_url) %>% unique() plan(multisession, workers = 4) safe_get_item_details <- safely(get_item_details) aub_details_raw <- aub_urls %>% future_map( \(x) { safe_result <- safe_get_item_details(item_url = x, stages = TRUE) safe_result$item_url <- x safe_result }, .progress = TRUE, .options = furrr_options(packages = c("ParlAT", "purrr", "tibble")) ) plan(sequential) aub_success_n <- sum(map_lgl(aub_details_raw, \(x) is.null(x$error))) if (aub_success_n == 0) { stop(paste0( "All ", length(aub_details_raw), " committee-report requests failed; the existing AUB cache was not overwritten. ", "First error: ", conditionMessage(aub_details_raw[[1]]$error) )) } readr::write_rds( aub_details_raw, here::here("posts", "2026-06-08-ParlAT-votingPatterns-2", "_data", "aub_details_raw.rds") ) ``` ::: ### Build committee votes from the reports Now I turn the committee reports into usable committee votes. For each report I do two things: a) read its `stages` and keep the row whose `stage_name` matches `Antrag auf Annahme des Gesetzesvorschlags` (which holds the `Dafür`/`Dagegen` party split — the actual vote), and b) resolve its `references` to find the row typed `HG` and follow that row's `url` back to the parent bill, exactly as demonstrated above for XXVII/I/2666. That `HG` reference is the *only* link between a report and its bill anywhere in the data: there's no shared numeric ID between the two pages, and titles aren't guaranteed to match character-for-character either (reports sometimes shorten or reformat a bill's title), so `references$url` is the one connection actually worth trusting. The result is one committee-vote row per bill, carrying the parent bill's identifiers so it slots in alongside the second- and third-reading rows further down. Three places let rows silently drop out of this link — `filter()` and `inner_join()` don't warn when they discard rows, so it's worth being explicit about all of them: - *No resolvable `HG` reference.* A handful of reports have no references at all, or none typed `HG` — `aub_parent`'s `map_chr()` returns `NA` for these, and `aub_committee_stages` drops them via `filter(!is.na(parent_url))`. - *The resolved parent isn't one of our own bills.* Even once a report resolves an `HG` url, that url has to match an `item_url` already present in `parent_meta` — i.e. a bill we actually fetched at the very start of this post. `committee_rows`'s `inner_join(parent_meta, ...)` drops any report whose parent isn't found there — for instance a report belonging to a non-`RV` item, which falls outside this post's scope. - *The bill was bundled into another bill's report as a co-subject.* A few hundred reports carry `MG` ('Mitgegenstand') references alongside their `HG`. A bill that appears only as somebody else's `MG` never resolves as an `HG` parent, so it gets no committee row at all — its committee vote was taken as part of a bundle rather than on its own. I don't try to recover these. One simplification is worth naming as well: a small number of reports (22 in the current data) carry *more than one* `HG` reference, i.e. they adopt several main subjects at once. `hg$url[1]` takes the first, so the committee vote is attributed to just one of them. Fixing this properly would mean fanning the report's vote out across every `HG` it names; given how few reports are affected I've left the simplification in place, but it is a simplification, not a non-issue. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Extract committee votes from reports and link them to the parent bill"} # successful report fetches; retain the requested URL if an older cached result # does not yet include the normalised item_url column aub_details <- aub_details_raw |> keep(\(x) is.null(x$error)) |> map(\(x) { result <- x$result if (!"item_url" %in% names(result)) { result$item_url <- x$item_url } result }) |> list_rbind() # link each report to its parent bill via the reference flagged "HG" (Hauptgegenstand) aub_parent <- aub_details |> transmute( aub_url = item_url, parent_url = map_chr(references, \(r) { if (is.null(r) || !is.data.frame(r) || nrow(r) == 0) { return(NA_character_) } hg <- r[!is.na(r$art) & r$art == "HG", , drop = FALSE] if (nrow(hg) == 0) { return(NA_character_) } # [1]: a handful of reports adopt several main subjects at once and carry multiple HG # rows; this attributes the vote to the first of them (see the caveat above) paste0("https://www.parlament.gv.at", hg$url[1]) }) ) # the committee's adoption-vote stage(s) from each report, linked to the parent bill aub_committee_stages <- aub_details |> select(aub_url = item_url, stages) |> filter(map_lgl(stages, \(x) !is.null(x))) |> unnest(stages) |> filter(str_detect( stage_name, regex("Antrag auf Annahme des", ignore_case = TRUE) )) |> mutate(stage_date = lubridate::dmy(stage_date)) |> left_join(aub_parent, by = "aub_url") |> filter(!is.na(parent_url)) # parent bill's item-level fields, so committee rows line up with the reading rows. # Sourced from item_details rather than item_stages: a bill that returned no stage data # is absent from item_stages and would silently lose its committee vote, even though it # is in scope. (No bill is affected in the current data, but the join key should not # depend on the bill happening to have stage rows.) parent_meta <- item_details |> distinct( item_url, legis_period, type_doc, title, item_number, status_number, status_description ) # one committee row per bill (keep the latest adoption vote if a report has several) committee_rows <- aub_committee_stages |> inner_join(parent_meta, by = c("parent_url" = "item_url")) |> transmute( item_url = parent_url, legis_period, type_doc, title, item_number, status_number, status_description, stage_date, stage_name, phase = "Ausschussbericht", reading = "committee" ) |> slice_max(stage_date, n = 1, by = item_url, with_ties = FALSE) nrow(committee_rows) # committee votes available to merge with the readings ## [1] 2571 ``` ::: Here's what that produces for our running example: a single committee-vote row for XXVII/I/2608, carrying the adoption-vote text straight from its report — the `Dagegen` list on this row is exactly where the FPÖ's committee-stage opposition (before it flips at the second reading) comes from. ::: {.column-margin} ![The committee report's own page, listing its stages. Click to enlarge. [link](https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2666){target="_blank"}](_img/AusschussErneuerbarLink.png) ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show the committee vote row retrieved for the example item"} example_committee_row <- committee_rows %>% filter(item_url == example_item_url) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false" code-summary="Committee vote row"} glimpse(example_committee_row) ## Rows: 1 ## Columns: 11 ## $ item_url "https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608" ## $ legis_period "XXVII" ## $ type_doc "RV" ## $ title "Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz, Änderung" ## $ item_number "2608 d.B." ## $ status_number 5 ## $ status_description "Beschlossen im Bundesrat 1016/BNR\nDafür: ÖVP, SPÖ, FPÖ, GRÜNE, dagegen: OF\nBeschlossen im Nationalrat 1016/BNR, Dafür: ÖVP, SPÖ, FPÖ, GRÜNE, dagegen: OF" ## $ stage_date 2024-06-26 ## $ stage_name "Ausschuss für Wirtschaft, Industrie und Energie: Antrag auf Annahme des unveränderten Gesetzesvorschlags\nDafür: ÖVP, GRÜNE, dagegen: SPÖ, FPÖ, NEOS" ## $ phase "Ausschussbericht" ## $ reading "committee" ``` ::: ## Combine committee votes with the readings The committee votes are ready, one clean row per bill. The reading votes are not: the stage data fetched back in *Data on the readings* still holds **every** procedural step, votes and non-votes alike. So this section does two things — narrow that stage data down to the actual reading votes, and then **bind the two sides together** into the finalized dataset the rest of this post analyzes. ### Scope the ordinary readings First the narrowing. I reduce the bills' own second- and third-reading stages down to just the rows where a vote was actually cast — a finished, vote-rows-only dataset for the "ordinary" readings. Along the way a `reading` column is added, recording the stage: second or third reading (or, in some cases, second and third at once). A second column, `vote_report_type`, is added one step later, once the committee rows have been bound on, since it applies to both sides alike. Note that this filter keeps only stages whose description actually carries vote-outcome text. That is a substantial cut — a large majority of the discarded rows are entries like '*NN. Sitzung des Nationalrates: Zweite und dritte Lesung*' which record that the readings happened but report no outcome at all, so there is nothing to extract a party position from. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show" code-summary="Filter to NR readings and vote-outcome text — the ordinary, committee-free dataset"} items_scope_ordinary <- item_stages |> filter(str_detect(phase, regex("NR"))) %>% # keep only National Council (NR) phases # plenary 2nd/3rd readings from the bill's own stages # r? makes the pattern match both "zweite"/"zweiter" and "dritte"/"dritter". # ignore_case is required: stage names capitalise the ordinal after a colon, e.g. # "141. Sitzung des Nationalrates: Zweite Lesung", and those rows are real readings. filter(str_detect(stage_name, regex("(dritter?|zweiter?) Lesung", ignore_case = TRUE))) %>% mutate( reading = case_when( # some items combine both readings into a single stage entry. # these patterns must be case-insensitive for the same reason as the filter above — # otherwise "Zweite und dritte Lesung" would fall through to the "dritte" branch str_detect(stage_name, regex("zweite", ignore_case = TRUE)) & str_detect(stage_name, regex("dritte", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "second & third", str_detect(stage_name, regex("zweite", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "second", str_detect(stage_name, regex("dritte", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "third", .default = NA_character_ ) ) %>% # keep only stages that contain actual vote-outcome text — this is now a finished, # vote-rows-only dataset for the ordinary (non-committee) readings. # same keyword set defined once further above, reused here rather than re-typed filter(str_detect( stage_name, regex(committee_vote_keywords, ignore_case = TRUE) )) nrow(items_scope_ordinary) # finished, committee-free vote dataset ## [1] 5221 ``` ::: For our running example, `items_scope_ordinary` now holds exactly the second- and third-reading rows — nothing else, and no committee row yet. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show the example item's rows in the finished, committee-free vote dataset"} example_vote_rows_ordinary <- items_scope_ordinary %>% filter(item_url == example_item_url) %>% select(title, stage_date, reading, stage_name) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false" code-summary="Example item's vote rows before committee is brought in"} example_vote_rows_ordinary ## # A tibble: 2 × 4 ## title stage_date reading stage_name ## ## 1 Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz, Änderung 2024-07-04 second "272. Sitzung des Nationalrates: Gesetzesvorschlag in zweiter Lesung angenommen\nDafür: ÖVP, FPÖ, GRÜNE, dagegen: SPÖ, NEOS" ## 2 Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz, Änderung 2024-07-04 third "272. Sitzung des Nationalrates: Gesetzesvorschlag in dritter Lesung angenommen\nDafür: ÖVP, SPÖ, FPÖ, GRÜNE, dagegen: NEOS" ``` ::: ### Bind on the committee votes Now the merge. `committee_rows` is already vote-rows-only by construction (see *Build committee votes from the reports* above — only the adoption-vote stage was ever kept), and `items_scope_ordinary` has just been reduced to vote rows too. The committee step is the bill's first formal vote, taken before it reaches the plenary floor; including it lets us follow an item across three stages instead of two. `vote_report_type` is classified on the combined table, giving `items_scope` — the combined set of vote rows. Two cleaning steps still follow below: items with duplicated stage rows are dropped, and the analysis then keeps only the `regular` vote-report type (the one whose text lists parties explicitly, and so the only one a party-level position can be read from). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show" code-summary="Bind on committee votes and classify vote report type"} items_scope <- items_scope_ordinary %>% bind_rows(committee_rows) %>% mutate( # classify how the vote result is reported; order matters — "regular" must come first # because some stage names contain both "dafür" and other keywords vote_report_type = case_when( # "regular" requires the explicit Dafür:/Dagegen: party-list separator the parser # keys on; parenthetical forms like "mehrstimmig (dafür S,V dagegen F)" fall through. # note "dafür:" *with* the colon: fn_get_votes() errors out on any row lacking it, # so the classifier has to guarantee that precondition rather than merely happen to str_detect(stage_name, regex("dafür:", ignore_case = TRUE)) & str_detect(stage_name, regex("dagegen", ignore_case = TRUE)) & str_detect( stage_name, regex(",\\s*dagegen:|\\.\\s*Dagegen:", ignore_case = TRUE) ) ~ "regular", str_detect( stage_name, regex("wechselnde Mehrheit", ignore_case = TRUE) ) ~ "wechselnde Mehrheit", str_detect( stage_name, regex("namentliche Abstimmung", ignore_case = TRUE) ) ~ "namentliche Abstimmung", str_detect( stage_name, regex("getrennte Abstimmung", ignore_case = TRUE) ) ~ "getrennte Abstimmung", str_detect(stage_name, regex("abgelehnt", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "abgelehnt", str_detect( stage_name, regex("mehrstimmig", ignore_case = TRUE) ) ~ "mehrstimmig", .default = NA ) ) nrow(items_scope) # vote rows after binding committee votes onto the readings ## [1] 7792 nrow(item_stages) # for comparison: all stage rows, votes and non-votes alike ## [1] 67252 ``` ::: And here's the payoff for our running example: the finalized, merged view — committee, second and third reading side by side for the same bill. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show the example item's rows in the finalized, merged dataset"} example_vote_rows_combined <- items_scope %>% filter(item_url == example_item_url) %>% select(reading, stage_date, vote_report_type, stage_name) %>% arrange(factor(reading, levels = c("committee", "second", "third"))) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false" code-summary="Example item's rows, combined"} example_vote_rows_combined ## Now that the analysis spans up to three stages — committee, second reading and third reading — an item no longer needs to have a fixed number of rows. Any item with more than one row for the same stage points to a data inconsistency (duplicates in the source, or an item that was approved/rejected twice within one stage). Others appear multiple times because an item was partly approved and partly rejected within one single reading, and hence got two rows in the data source, as in [XXVIII/I/403](https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVIII/I/403). Rather than trying to repair these inconsistencies one by one, I simply remove the affected items from the analysis. Subsequently, I narrow the data down to items with a 'regular' vote report. A second duplicate check follows the type filter — it is purely defensive and in practice finds nothing, since taking a subset of rows cannot create a duplicate that wasn't already there — but it makes the invariant explicit rather than assumed. The last line below shows which share of the original vote stages survives all these filters. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show" code-summary="Remove items with duplicate stage rows, keep regular vote type only"} # drop items that had duplicate rows within a stage; only clean items remain items_scope_pairs <- items_scope %>% anti_join(., dup_rows, by = c("legis_period", "item_url")) nrow(items_scope_pairs) ## [1] 7745 # sanity check: no item should now have more than one row per stage items_scope_pairs %>% count(legis_period, item_url, reading, name = "n_rows") %>% filter(n_rows > 1) %>% nrow() ## [1] 0 table(items_scope_pairs$reading) ## ## committee second second & third third ## 2562 2586 8 2589 # this analysis focuses only on "regular" votes (explicit Dafür/Dagegen party lists) items_scope_pairs_regular <- items_scope_pairs %>% filter(vote_report_type == "regular") # defensive re-check after the type filter. A row subset of an already-unique table cannot # contain new duplicates, so this is expected to be empty — assert that rather than silently # anti_join()ing against nothing, which would hide it if the invariant ever did break dup_rows2 <- items_scope_pairs_regular %>% count(legis_period, item_url, reading, name = "n_rows") %>% filter(n_rows > 1) stopifnot(nrow(dup_rows2) == 0) nrow(items_scope_pairs_regular) # vote rows left after keeping only "regular" reports ## [1] 6783 nrow(items_scope_pairs_regular) / nrow(items_scope) # share of all vote stages covered ## [1] 0.8705082 ``` ::: ## Extract votes Now to the heart of the matter: getting each party's position out of the stage description. The text follows (mostly) the pattern 'Dafür: party A, party B, dagegen: party C', so the function below splits the string at the 'dagegen' boundary and cleans up both sides. Two details are worth mentioning: first, I keep only tokens which appear in a predefined list of valid party labels — this guards against vote counts, footnotes and other non-party fragments sneaking into the results. Second, since party labels changed over the legislative periods (e.g. the FPÖ appearing as 'F' in earlier periods), a small helper maps the historical variants onto one canonical name per party. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Define party normalisation and Dafür/Dagegen vote text parser"} # includes historical aliases (F, NEOS-LIF, F-BZÖ, S/V/N/G single-letter forms) # alongside canonical modern names; used as an allowlist to filter out non-party tokens valid_parties <- c( "SPÖ", "ÖVP", "F", "FPÖ", "GRÜNE", "L", "BZÖ", "STRONACH", "NEOS", "NEOS-LIF", "F-BZÖ", "JETZT", "PILZ", "NEOS/NEOS-LIF", "JETZT/PILZ", "S", "V", "N", "G", "T", # Team Stronach, single-letter form "J", # JETZT, single-letter form "B" # BZÖ, single-letter form ) # maps historical/transitional party labels to a single canonical name per party normalise_party <- function(party) { case_when( party %in% c("NEOS-LIF", "NEOS/NEOS-LIF") ~ "NEOS", party %in% c("JETZT", "PILZ", "JETZT/PILZ", "J") ~ "JETZT/PILZ", party == "F" ~ "FPÖ", party %in% c("F-BZÖ", "B") ~ "BZÖ", party == "S" ~ "SPÖ", party == "V" ~ "ÖVP", party == "N" ~ "NEOS", party == "G" ~ "GRÜNE", party == "T" ~ "STRONACH", TRUE ~ party ) } fn_get_votes <- function(vt) { # inner helper: splits a raw comma-separated party string into a clean character vector clean_parties <- function(x) { if (is.na(x) || str_trim(x) == "-") { return(character(0)) } x |> str_split(",\\s*") |> unlist() |> str_trim() |> # drop any parenthetical qualifier and keep the party label in front of it, e.g. # "SPÖ (Mehrheit)" -> "SPÖ", "GRÜNE (G tw." -> "GRÜNE", "BZÖ ( dafür Andere" -> "BZÖ". # This must strip from the opening paren: removing only a trailing ")" would leave # "SPÖ (Mehrheit", which fails the all-caps test below and silently loses the party. str_remove("\\s*\\(.*$") |> str_remove("\\)+$") |> # stray closing paren with no opener in this token str_trim() |> # keep only all-caps tokens (party abbreviations); drops vote counts, notes, etc. keep(\(p) { str_detect( p, regex("^[[:upper:]ÄÖÜ]+(?:[-/][[:upper:]ÄÖÜ]+)*$") ) }) |> keep(\(p) p %in% valid_parties) # final guard against unknown tokens } # some stage texts use ". Dagegen:" (period separator) instead of ", dagegen:" # normalise to a consistent comma form so the split below works in both cases vt_norm <- str_replace( vt, regex("\\.\\s*Dagegen:", ignore_case = TRUE), ", dagegen:" ) # split at the dagegen boundary; n=2 prevents splitting inside party lists parts <- str_split( vt_norm, regex(",\\s*dagegen:", ignore_case = TRUE), n = 2 )[[1]] if (length(parts) != 2) { stop("Regular vote text does not contain both Dafür and Dagegen parts.") } if (!str_detect(parts[1], regex("Dafür:", ignore_case = TRUE))) { stop("Regular vote text does not contain a Dafür part.") } # strip the "Dafür:" label and everything before it (dotall handles multi-line stage names) yes_raw <- parts[1] |> str_remove(regex("^.*Dafür:\\s*", dotall = TRUE, ignore_case = TRUE)) # parts[2] runs to the end of the string, so a *second* Dafür:/Dagegen: pair — e.g. # "dagegen: F (f dafür: Dr. Ofner)" — would otherwise leak that vote's parties into the # no-list once the parenthetical strip above keeps the leading token. ' width=100%} ::: ::: # Results Where along an item's journey does a party actually change its mind — between the committee vote and the second reading, or between the second and the third reading? This is where the accommodation of opposition parties should become visible: if a governing majority makes concessions to win broader support, the resulting position changes should cluster at a particular stage. Below I prepare a tidy table of every transition and then work through it in five steps: the **number** of flips by legislative period and direction; where flips concentrate by party, first as absolute counts, then as each party's share of its period's movement, and then measured against the bills each party could actually have moved on; and a compact summary of which stage carries most of the movement. A final section leaves the aggregates behind and lists the individual bills where a position actually changed. One structural point to keep in mind throughout, because it shapes the central result before any data is involved: the second and third readings of a bill are normally taken in the **same sitting, minutes apart**, whereas the committee vote happens days or weeks earlier, in a different room, with time for negotiation in between. So the two transitions are not comparable windows of opportunity. If it turns out that almost nothing moves between the second and third reading, that is in large part *mechanical* — there is barely any interval in which a position could change — and not evidence that parliamentary debate never persuades anyone. Read the committee → second reading step as "what happened between committee and the floor", and the second → third step as "what happened during a single sitting". A note on denominators, since the charts below use more than one. Counts are counts — the first chart simply reports how many changes occurred, which makes periods with more (or more contested) bills look busier for that reason alone. Where a percentage *is* shown, it is a composition rather than a rate: the party tiles divide that period's own position changes between the parties and add up to 100% within a column. That answers "who moved", not "how often a party moves" — a party with a large share may have moved once in a quiet period. The stage × period tile at the end is the one genuine rate, dividing flips by all comparable pairs. That leaves one thing the descriptive charts cannot tell you. A party that already voted *yes* at the earlier stage cannot flip *no → yes* — it was never in a position to make that move, so its absence from the counts is not evidence of immobility. Measuring movement against opportunity needs a denominator built from the position each party actually went in with, which is what the fourth chart does: it divides each party's changes by the bills it went into holding the prior position, separately for every party and period. The stage × period tile at the end is a coarser rate that does not condition this way, and reads accordingly. And a note on who counts as government: coalition membership is coded once per legislative period, which is an approximation. It is a poor one for GP XXVI in particular — that period covers the ÖVP-FPÖ coalition, its collapse after the Ibiza affair in May 2019, the subsequent ÖVP-only cabinet and the Bierlein caretaker government. Votes from the second half of GP XXVI are therefore labelled against a coalition that no longer existed, so the government/opposition split shown for that period should be read with care. GP XXII carries a milder version of the same problem: the FPÖ split in 2005 and its ministers continued in government as the BZÖ, so both are coded as governing for the whole period. That is why the coalition label on the axis of the stage × period chart further below reads 'ÖVP, FPÖ, BZÖ' for that one period — an artefact of period-level coding, not a three-party coalition. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Build shared party/period/government lookups, then encode positions per stage and classify each transition's change"} # align aliases before joining mutate(is_gov = TRUE) # tracks which party × period combinations actually appear in the data # used later to distinguish "not in parliament" (white) from "zero flips" (grey) party_period_presence <- items_scope_pairs_regular_wide %>% distinct(legis_period, party) %>% mutate(present = TRUE) all_parties <- union(party_period_presence$party, gov_parties_lookup$party) # One row per **party × legislative period × transition × direction**, never pooled, with each quantity the rest of the post draws on: - **At disposal** — the bills the party went into holding the prior position *and* which then reached the later stage. This is the denominator: the bills it genuinely could have changed its mind on. - **Changed** — how many of those it actually changed. - **Rate** — changed ÷ at disposal. - **No party-level record later** — bills the party held a position on where the later stage produced no vote naming the parties, so the party's position there cannot be observed. These are **excluded** from *At disposal*; the column is here so the adjustment is auditable rather than implicit. That exclusion is substantial — at the committee → 2nd reading step it removes about one in five of the positions a party took — and it is important not to misread it. These are almost never bills that died: of the 594 bills with no usable second-reading position, six had no second reading at all. The rest were read and voted, but in a form that names no parties, usually because the bill was split and voted in parts. Since such bills are disproportionately the contested ones, the rates below describe the plainly-decided bills and understate how much movement occurs overall. The table is searchable and sortable, and every column filters, so any number quoted anywhere in this post can be traced back to its row here. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Build the per-party opportunity/change table underlying every chart below"} # item-level: did the stage produce a vote that names the parties? Only six bills in # the whole dataset genuinely never had a second reading. item_stage_record <- items_scope_pairs_regular_wide %>% summarise( record_second = any(!is.na(yes_second) | !is.na(no_second)), record_third = any(!is.na(yes_third) | !is.na(no_third)), .by = item_url ) # one row per party x bill x transition, carrying the position going in, the position coming # out (NA if none was recorded) and whether the later stage produced a party-level record at all opportunity_base <- bind_rows( stage_positions %>% left_join(item_stage_record, by = "item_url") %>% transmute( item_url, legis_period, party, transition = "Committee → 2nd reading", from_pos = pos_committee, to_pos = pos_second, has_record = record_second ), stage_positions %>% left_join(item_stage_record, by = "item_url") %>% transmute( item_url, legis_period, party, transition = "2nd → 3rd reading", from_pos = pos_second, to_pos = pos_third, has_record = record_third ) ) %>% filter(!is.na(from_pos)) %>% # the party has to have held a position to be able to leave it mutate( # the only move the prior position makes possible direction = if_else(from_pos == "Dagegen", "no → yes", "yes → no"), at_disposal = !is.na(to_pos), changed = at_disposal & to_pos != from_pos ) opportunity_table_data <- opportunity_base %>% summarise( n_at_disposal = sum(at_disposal), n_changed = sum(changed), n_no_record = sum(!at_disposal & !has_record), .by = c(legis_period, party, transition, direction) ) %>% mutate(rate = if_else(n_at_disposal > 0, n_changed / n_at_disposal, NA_real_)) %>% arrange(legis_period, transition, direction, desc(n_changed)) # The table has to reconcile with `transitions`, which every chart is built from: same # denominators, same numerators. ``` ::: ::: ## Flip counts by period and direction The most direct answer. For each legislative period, the bars compare the **number** of position changes at the two transitions, split into the two directions (no → yes, a move toward support; yes → no, a withdrawal). The chart covers **opposition parties only**. Government parties are left out deliberately: across all nine periods there is exactly one government-party flip in the data, on three comparable pairs, so a rate for them is built on too little to plot and an absolute bar for them would be a single unit high. That near-total absence is itself worth stating — a party does not usually vote against the bill its own government tabled — but it is a sentence, not a panel. It's worth being precise about what a tall bar means, because the intuitive reading is the wrong way round. A flip at committee → 2nd reading means a party voted one way *in committee* and differently *on the floor* — so the position moved in the interval **between** the two, once the committee stage was already over. A deal actually struck inside the committee produces the opposite: the party votes yes there and yes again later, and contributes **no** flip at all. [Open on parlament.gv.at →](https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVIII/I/449) ::: # Wrap-up So, where does a party actually change its mind on a government bill? The short answer: **between the committee and the floor, and almost nowhere else**. Across 2,710 Regierungsvorlagen from the 20th to the 28th legislative period, 3.90% of the comparable party–bill pairs change position between the committee vote and the second reading (354 of 9,082), against 0.31% between the second and the third reading (30 of 9,695). That is 92.2% of all the movement in the data sitting in one of the two steps. Taking the three questions from the top in turn: **Between which stages?** Committee → second reading, overwhelmingly. But recall what that interval is and is not: the second and third readings are typically taken minutes apart in the same sitting, so the near-absence of movement there is substantially mechanical rather than a finding about plenary debate. The committee → second reading step is the one that actually contains days or weeks in which something could be negotiated — and it is the one where the changes show up. **Which parties?** In the 1,849-bill subset observable at all three stages, changes are almost exclusively an opposition phenomenon: 359 of the 360 recorded changes come from opposition parties. GRÜNE accounts for the largest single share (135), followed by the other long-serving opposition parties. That asymmetry is the expected shape if these flips are the trace of a governing majority buying support rather than of parties independently reconsidering the merits — a government party has little reason to vote against its own bill in committee in the first place. **Under which government?** Here I'd rather under-claim. The raw counts are highest in the earlier periods, but as flagged at the outset, legislative periods are not directly comparable: they differ in length, in how many bills they produced, and in how contested those bills were. A period with more `no` votes at the committee stage simply has more opportunities to flip. The per-period tiles show the pattern holding throughout, but I would not read the ranking between periods as a ranking of governmental responsiveness. One direction is worth flagging on its own. At the committee → second reading step, moves *toward* support outnumber withdrawals by roughly 2.3 to 1 (246 versus 108). Positions converge on their way to the floor far more often than they fracture. A closing caveat on what this does and does not show. These numbers locate *where* positions change; they cannot say *why*. A flip from no to yes is consistent with a concession having been made — that was the motivating hunch — but it is equally consistent with an opposition party simply being persuaded, or with the committee stage having clarified something the party had misread. Establishing the difference means reading the individual bill and what changed in it between the two votes. The table above links every case, so that check is at least available for anyone who wants to make it on a specific bill. Finally, the scope: this post covers government bills only. Items initiated inside the National Council follow a different political logic, and whether the same pattern holds for them is a separate question — and a good candidate for a Part III.
